current_example.title: Example: Evaluating Surface Integrals Using Polar Coordinates

q-161325.name: Question 1
q-161325.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={x}^{2}{z}^{2},$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161325.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=-2x,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})=4y.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-2x)}^{2}+{(4y)}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,{x}^{2}(-{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2})^{2}\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,({x}^{6}-4{y}^{2}{x}^{4}+4{y}^{4}{x}^{2})\sqrt{1+4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

q-161321.name: Question 2
q-161321.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=\sqrt{2}xyz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y$ for $-1\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161321.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)=-\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(-\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{2}xy(-\sqrt{2}x-\sqrt{2}y)\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,(-2{x}^{2}y-2x{y}^{2})\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,-2\sqrt{5}({x}^{2}y+x{y}^{2})\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

q-161327.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)={z}^{2},$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=x+\sqrt{2}y$ for $-1\le x\le 2$ and $-1\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\boxed{}\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161327.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{2}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{2}y)=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(1)}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,2(x+\sqrt{2}y)^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{2}{\int }_{-1}^{2}\,2({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}+2\sqrt{2}xy)\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

∂z∂x=∂∂x(x+2y)=1, and ∂z∂y=∂∂y(x+2y)=2.

q-161323.name: Question 5
q-161323.problem:
Consider the surface integral of the function $f(x,y,z)=-3xz,$ where the surface $S$ is defined by $z=\sqrt{2}x+\sqrt{2}y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 2.$
This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. 

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\boxed{}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x
$$

What is the missing expression?
q-161323.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(\sqrt{2}x+\sqrt{2}y)=\sqrt{2},
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(\sqrt{2}x+\sqrt{2}y)=\sqrt{2}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as 

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}+{(\sqrt{2})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,-3x(\sqrt{2}x+\sqrt{2}y)\sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2}\,-3\sqrt{10}({x}^{2}+xy)\,\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

?

Consider the surface integral of the function f(x,y,z)=−3xz, where the surface S is defined by z=2x+2y for 0≤x≤1 and 0≤y≤2. This surface integral can be written as a repeated integral, as shown below. ∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∫01∫02AAAAAAAdydx

What is the missing expression?

a
−35x(x2+x2y2)
b
−210(−x2y+xy)
c
−35(x2+2xy)
d
−310(x2+xy)
e
−103(x2−xy)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

For a surface S defined by z=g(x,y) with (x,y)∈D, the surface integral of a scalar function f(x,y,z) over S is given by

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA.

For the partial derivatives, we have

∂z∂x=∂∂x(2x+2y)=2, and ∂z∂y=∂∂y(2x+2y)=2.

Therefore, the surface integral can be written as

∬Sf(x,y,z)dS=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(∂z∂x)2+(∂z∂y)2dA=∬Df(x,y,g(x,y))1+(2)2+(2)2dA=∬D−3x(2x+2y)5dA=∫01∫02−310(x2+xy)dydx.

q-161350.name: Question 7
q-161350.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}\sqrt{z}\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=y-3x$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $3x\le y\le 3.$
q-161350.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(y-3x)=-3,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(y-3x)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\sqrt{z}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{y-3x}\sqrt{1+(-3)^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{y-3x}\sqrt{11}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{11}{∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{y-3x}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{11}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{3x}^{3}\sqrt{y-3x}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{11}{\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{2}{3}(y-3x)^{3/2}]}_{y=3x}^{y=3}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(3-3x)^{3/2}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{2\sqrt{11}}{3}\,{[\frac{2}{5}\cdot (-\frac{1}{3})(3-3x)^{5/2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{45}(0-{3}^{5/2}) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{11}}{45}(9\sqrt{3}) \\  & =\frac{4\sqrt{33}}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

q-160836.problem:
Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}12xyz\,\text{d}S
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0\le x\le 1$ and $0\le y\le 1.$
q-160836.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+y)=1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}12xyz\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,12xy(x+y)\sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,12xy(x+y)\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{∬}_{D}\,12{x}^{2}y+12x{y}^{2}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(12{x}^{2}y+12x{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}[6{x}^{2}{y}^{2}+4x{y}^{3}]_{y=0}^{y=1}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{1}(6{x}^{2}+4x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\sqrt{3}\,[2{x}^{3}+2{x}^{2}]_{0}^{1} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(2+2)-0 \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x+y)=1.
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\frac{z-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{(2x+y)-y}{\sqrt{6}y}\sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+{1}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\,\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{\int }_{1}^{e}\frac{2x}{y}\,\text{d}y\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x[\operatorname{ln}⁡y]_{y=1}^{y=e}\,\text{d}x \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x \\  & =[{x}^{2}]_{1}^{2} \\  & =4-1 \\  & =3\end{aligned}

$$

Evaluate the surface integral 

$$
{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=x+\sqrt{3}y$ whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
q-161322.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=1,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{1}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{5}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,{e}^{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

$$

{∬}_{S}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S,
$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=4x+\sqrt{3}y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $1$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
q-161338.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+\sqrt{3}y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+\sqrt{3}y)=\sqrt{3}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{3})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{20}\,\text{d}A \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 1,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{D}\,(1-{x}^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{∬}_{Δ}(1-{r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta -{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{1}(r-{r}^{3})\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{2}}{2}-\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =2\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\frac{1}{4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{5}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

q-161328.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(4x+\sqrt{8}y)=4,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(4x+\sqrt{8}y)=\sqrt{8}.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot \sqrt{1+{4}^{2}+(\sqrt{8})^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\cdot 5\,\text{d}A \\  & =5{∬}_{D}\,\sqrt{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$

$$

where $S$ is defined by $z=2x-y$ and whose domain is the circle of radius $2$ centered at $O,$ as shown above.
q-161302.worked_solution:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

$$
{∬}_{S}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}S={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A.
$$

For the partial derivatives, we have

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂x}=\frac{∂}{∂x}(2x-y)=2,
$$

and

$$
\frac{∂z}{∂y}=\frac{∂}{∂y}(2x-y)=-1.
$$

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{S}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}S & ={∬}_{D}f(x,y,g(x,y))\sqrt{1+{(\frac{∂z}{∂x})}^{2}+{(\frac{∂z}{∂y})}^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{1+{2}^{2}+(-1)^{2}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\cdot \sqrt{6}\,\text{d}A \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A.\end{aligned}
$$

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r,\theta ),$ our domain can be expressed as 

$$
Δ=\{(r,\theta )\,:\,0\le r\le 2,\,0\le \theta \le 2\pi \}.
$$

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta $ and $y=r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta ,$ we obtain 

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{6}{∬}_{D}\,({x}^{2}+{y}^{2})\,\text{d}A & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(r\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta ,r\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta )\,r\text{ }drd\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{∬}_{Δ}({r}^{2}{cos}^{2}⁡\theta +{r}^{2}{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )\cdot r\text{d}r\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{\int }_{0}^{2}{r}^{3}\,\text{d}r\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{[\frac{{r}^{4}}{4}]}_{0}^{2}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{6}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =4\sqrt{6}[\theta ]_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =8\sqrt{6}\pi .\end{aligned}
$$
